summary:
Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes stands under the French national framework. No region-specific signal was identified: the region's own page carries no trans-specific content, and no regional deviation from the national position was located in the source inventory.

Prison placement follows no statutory rule. Article D248 of the criminal procedure code assigns detainees according to the sex inscribed on their identity documents, and each facility improvises around that rule. A BuzzFeed News feature of 12 January 2018, 'The Plight Of Trans Women In Prison', reports first-person accounts of placement in all-male facilities, including a three-day stay in Lille's men's prison in 2014 marked by detainee and staff hostility, and the story of an Argentinian trans woman's incarceration. The feature also covers the well-publicised case of a US trans woman detained in poor conditions after a 2016 Paris protest case.

The controller-general of places of deprivation of liberty states that transgender detainees are the group that suffers the most in prison.

The CGLPL opinion of 25 May 2021, issued by the Contrôleur général des lieux de privation de liberté, examines the treatment of transgender persons in all places of deprivation of liberty. It rests on about forty referrals received since 2010, interviews with trans associations and European experts, and five on-site inspections covering Fleury-Mérogis men's and women's prisons, Caen, Saint-Martin-de-Ré, Toulouse-Seysses and the Toulouse central police station, where eight trans women and one trans man were interviewed. The opinion finds persistent serious violations of the fundamental rights of trans detainees, including isolation and overcrowding risks, and recommends that the 2016 depathologising law, which removed the surgery requirement for civil-status change, be translated into prison regulations. Its scope explicitly extends to intersex and non-binary people.

For partner recognition, France legalised same-sex marriage and full adoption in 2013, and civil solidarity pacts have existed since 1999. A trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship therefore encounters a recognised legal baseline.

Penal Code article 225-1 has covered gender identity since an 18 November 2016 amendment that replaced 'sexual identity', protected since 2012. Homophobic hate speech has carried penalties of up to EUR 45,000 and/or one year's imprisonment since a 31 December 2004 amendment.

On legal gender recognition, a bill approved by the Senate on 6 November 2015 and by the National Assembly on 24 May 2016 was signed into law on 18 November 2016 and took effect on 1 January 2017. It abolished the sex-reassignment-surgery and forced-sterilisation requirements, rejected a Senate amendment that would have demanded proof of medical treatment, and requires going before a court rather than any medical intervention.

Transsexualism is classed under long-term-illness ALD 31, so gender-affirming treatment is funded by the Sécurité Sociale.
tangentialFactors:
The national layer records detention and the border as the two settings where documented risk concentrates for trans travellers in France, with persistent discrimination rather than legal prohibition in everyday movement, accommodation and services. That national assessment applies in Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes; the region adds no separate turbulence signal of its own.

The CGLPL's on-site inspections named in the inventory (Fleury-Mérogis, Caen, Saint-Martin-de-Ré, Toulouse-Seysses, Toulouse central police station) sit outside Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes, so they illustrate the national pattern rather than regional practice.
localsOnly:
Residents of Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes are subject to the same national rules on documents, protection and care as any trans person in France: Article D248 placement by the sex on identity documents, court-based legal gender recognition in force since 1 January 2017, ALD 31 coverage funding gender-affirming treatment through the Sécurité Sociale, and Penal Code article 225-1 protection for gender identity.

The CGLPL opinion of 25 May 2021 is binding guidance for all places of deprivation of liberty in France, including any facility in the region, and recommends that the 2016 depathologising law be written into prison regulations.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether any prison, police station or border post within Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes has been inspected by the CGLPL, or has received referrals from trans detainees, is unresolved: the inventory names only facilities outside the region.

No regional authority, oversight body or incident specific to Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes is sourced here; the French-language Wikipedia entry for the region yielded no usable finding. Regional enforcement practice at Lyon or Grenoble airports and in regional accommodation is not sourced.
